explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, David, Israel's king. Jesus asks, "How can it be said that the Christ is the Son of David?" Everything in this little puzzle hangs on that name. Keep your eye on it, because David is about to speak for himself.

Saul was a king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), but he's not the king Jesus names. Jesus asks how the Christ can be the son of David. Think of a name stamped on a cookie. Stamp the wrong one and the whole batch says something else. Here the name is David.

Ahab was a king of Israel too (1 Kings 16:29), but Jesus doesn't bring him up here. The king in His question is David. He asks how the Christ can be called David's son, and then He backs it up with David's own words. Ahab just wandered in from another chapter.

That's it. In the psalm the Lord says to the one at His right hand, "…until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet." See the "I"? The Lord is the one doing the making. The one at His right hand gets to sit while the Lord handles it.

explanations.answer: The one at His right hand
explanations.explanation: That's an easy mix-up, because that person is in the middle of the sentence. But look at who says "I." The Lord says, "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet." So the Lord does the making, and the one at His right hand just sits there. Easiest job in the kitchen.

Nope, no soldiers show up in this verse. Jesus quotes David saying, "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet." The one who says "I make" is the Lord. Nobody else is handed that job, mighty men or not.

Right, Lord. Jesus says, "Thus David calls Him 'Lord.'" Now hold that next to the question of how the Christ can also be David's son. Jesus leaves that question hanging out there for everyone to chew on.

I get why you went there, since the whole question starts with "Son of David." But in the psalm David doesn't call the Christ his son. Jesus says, "Thus David calls Him 'Lord.'" That's the part that makes the question so interesting.
Servant would flip things around, and it's not what the text has. Jesus says David calls Him "Lord." That's the word that makes Jesus ask, "So how can He be David's son?" You can't skip it, friend.

Long robes, yes. Jesus says the scribes "like to walk around in long robes." Notice He says they like walking around in them. I think they were doing a lot of strolling. If I had a robe that fancy, my apron would be jealous.
Sackcloth is scratchy, and that's the opposite of what Jesus describes. He says the scribes "like to walk around in long robes." Nothing about itchy outfits. The scribes picked the long robes.

Camel's hair does show up in the Bible. John the Baptist's clothes were made of it (Matthew 3:4). But that's John, not the scribes. About the scribes, Jesus says they like to walk around in long robes.

It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says the scribes love "the chief seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets." Those are the best seats in the house, not the lowest. The lowest seats weren't on their wish list.
False is right. Jesus says they love "the places of honor at banquets." He says they love the chief seats in the synagogues too. These folks were aiming for the front, not the back row.

Yes. Jesus says they "for a show make lengthy prayers." So the length was part of the performance. That's right alongside defrauding widows of their houses. It's a heavy part of what Jesus says, so I'll just say it plainly.
Rain doesn't come up anywhere in this passage. Jesus says the scribes "for a show make lengthy prayers." The point is the show. He says it right after saying they defraud widows of their houses.

I wish that were true, friend, but Jesus says the opposite. The scribes "defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers." The prayers are for a show, not for the widows. I think that stings, and I'd rather say so than skip past it.
Not quite. Jesus says, "These men will receive greater condemnation." That's not a reward at all. He says it right after naming what they do. It's a serious word, so it's worth reading slowly.

False is right. Jesus says, "These men will receive greater condemnation." He says it right after naming what they do to widows and how they pray for show. The text says what the outcome is, and it's not a reward.

Yes, and this is the part that gets me. Jesus says, "this poor widow has put in more than all the others." He says "Truly I tell you" first, so He wants everyone to hear it. Two small copper coins, and He says she put in more than the rest.

I know it sounds backwards, but it's true. Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others." The two small copper coins look tiny next to the rich people's gifts. Jesus counts it differently, and that's the whole point of the scene.

explanations.answer: She put in all she had to live on
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says the others gave out of their surplus, "but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on." Jesus says what made hers more, and it wasn't the size of the coins. I think about that every time I count my crumbs.

explanations.answer: Her two coins were old and very rare
explanations.explanation: The text never says a thing about the coins being rare. They're called two small copper coins. Jesus gives the reason Himself: "she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on." It was about what she had, not what the coins were worth to a collector.

explanations.answer: She gave in secret and told no one
explanations.explanation: The passage doesn't say anything about secrecy. It says Jesus saw her put in the coins, and then He gave His reason. He says, "she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on." That's the reason, and it's the only one He gives.

Surplus is it. Jesus says, "they all contributed out of their surplus." That means what they had left over. Then He sets her beside them: she gave out of her poverty. Think of a cookie jar. They gave from the extras, and she gave from the bottom of it.
Wages never comes up in this passage. Jesus says the others "contributed out of their surplus." That's the word to remember. He says it right before He mentions what she gave out of her poverty.
The text doesn't mention an inheritance. Jesus says, "they all contributed out of their surplus." That means what they had extra. Then He says she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.
